title: The Ledger of Little Hawley
premise: When a stranger's body is found on the marsh road outside Little Hawley, dressed entirely in clothes stolen from retired detective Ada Villalobos's own closet, the town that once shunned her turns to her for answers. The victim clutched a page from an old shop ledger — Ada's own ledger, the one she inherited with the bookshop and never fully read. As she decodes its cipher, she discovers it records not sales but payments: seven years of hush money keeping the town's darkest secret buried, and her name at the bottom of every page. The killer is the one person who has been quietly protecting Ada all along, and the final entry names the next payment due: her.
about_author: Petra Kavanagh is the pen name of a former small-town bookseller who spent a decade listening to gossip over the register before turning it into fiction. She writes mysteries about places that keep secrets the way other towns keep gardens — carefully, and out of sight.

chapters.title: The Weight of Borrowed Clothes
chapters.summary: Ada Villalobos opens her failing bookshop on a gray October morning, cataloging debts and dodging the landlord's calls. When Constable Reyes arrives asking her to identify clothing found on a body — her own cardigan, her own scarf — her careful, alphabetized life cracks open. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: A Stranger in Sunday Shoes
chapters.summary: At the marsh road scene, Ada recognizes nothing about the dead man except what he wore. His shoes are polished; his hands are soft; he carried no identification but a torn page of handwriting in a cipher she almost recognizes. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: uncanny disorientation — grief for someone she never knew.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Counter
chapters.summary: Ada digs out the shop's original ledger, inherited with the store seven years ago, and matches the torn page to its missing corner. The columns aren't sales. They're dates, initials, and sums — including entries dated after the previous owner's death. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: the thrill of competence returning like an old ache.

chapters.title: Everyone Knew Him Except Me
chapters.summary: In the village pub, Ada probes for the victim's identity while noticing how quickly conversations die when she approaches. Old-timer Winn Hale warns her, kindly, to leave the ledger alone. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: loneliness sharpening into suspicion — the town is a closed fist around something.

chapters.title: Initials in Red Ink
chapters.summary: Working late, Ada decodes the first layer: the initials correspond to nine townspeople, each receiving regular payments. Her own initials appear as recipient, not payer — going back to the week she arrived. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: vertigo; her whole new life may have been purchased.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Wore My Face
chapters.summary: A nervous drifter named Colm Okafor comes forward claiming he saw the body dumped — and that the killer wore Ada's coat. His account is too precise in some details, blank in others. POV shift: Colm. Emotional beat: fear of being believed by the wrong person.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Small Kindnesses
chapters.summary: Ada retraces her arrival in Little Hawley: the impossibly cheap lease, the anonymous loan that saved the shop, the neighbors' slow thaw. Each kindness now reads as a transaction. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: grief for a belonging that may have been bought.

chapters.title: What the Marsh Keeps
chapters.summary: Ada and Colm search the marsh near where the body was found and uncover a buried strongbox containing cash and photographs of the nine payees — including one of Ada asleep in her shop. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: violation; the watcher was always close.

chapters.title: The Constable's Quiet Doubt
chapters.summary: Constable Reyes reveals the case file on the previous owner's death was sealed from above, and admits he requested it be reopened twice and was refused both times. He's either ally or bait. POV: Reyes. Emotional beat: institutional rot seen through one honest man's fatigue.

chapters.title: The Ninth Initial
chapters.summary: Ada identifies eight of the payees — all people who've protected or employed her. The ninth initial belongs to someone dead: the previous owner, Ruth Ellery, whose payments continued posthumously. Someone is spending a dead woman's money. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: the past refusing to stay filed.

chapters.title: Colm's Half-Truth
chapters.summary: Ada catches Colm burning a second ledger page he'd pocketed. He confesses he was paid to watch her shop and report visitors — by letters signed R.E., sent long after Ruth Ellery died. POV: Colm. Emotional beat: shame and the desperate hope of redemption through confession.

chapters.title: The Archive Room
chapters.summary: Following the paper trail to the county records office, Ada finds Ruth Ellery's sealed file: she wasn't the shopkeeper everyone remembered but a blackmailer who documented a fatal accident covered up by the town's founding families. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: horror reframed — the villain kept receipts.

chapters.title: The Accident at Hawley Weir
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, reconstructed from documents: twenty years ago, a young worker died at the weir and the death was ruled misadventure. Nine witnesses took money. Ruth Ellery saw everything. POV: alternating document fragments and Ada's narration. Emotional beat: the price of survival made literal.

chapters.title: Someone Is Paying Still
chapters.summary: Ada realizes the payments never stopped because the cover-up never ended: the drowned man had a child, now grown, asking questions. The victim on the marsh road was that child's investigator. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: moral inversion — the 'victim' town fears may be justice itself.

chapters.title: Locked In
chapters.summary: Ada's shop is ransacked overnight; the ledger is gone. She finds a note in Ruth Ellery's handwriting style — impossible unless the writer learned it — telling her to stop, or become an entry. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: terror arriving politely, on stationery.

chapters.title: The Person Who Fed Me
chapters.summary: Ada narrows the suspects to those with access to her home, her food, her habits across seven years. Every clue points toward the one person whose kindness predates even the ledger: her landlady, Edith March, Ruth Ellery's sister-in-law. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: betrayal tasting like every shared meal.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Confronted, Edith doesn't deny it — she explains: after Ruth's suspicious death, she took up the blackmail to protect the payees' families from ruin, and began paying Ada because Ruth's last letter warned Ada would be killed next. POV: Edith. Emotional beat: love weaponized into surveillance.

chapters.title: Edith's Confession, Part Two
chapters.summary: Edith admits she hired the investigator herself to finally end it — and that his murder means someone else is inside the arrangement, someone who wants the secret permanent. The real killer is still hidden among the nine. POV: Edith. Emotional beat: the protector unmasked as another prisoner.

chapters.title: The Trap Written Backwards
chapters.summary: Ada stages a fake ledger sale through Colm, offering the complete decoded ledger to the hidden player. The meet is set at the derelict Hawley Weir. Reyes, half-trusting, agrees to shadow them. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: cold clarity — using the town's own currency, secrets, as bait.

chapters.title: High Water at the Weir
chapters.summary: At the weir, the killer is revealed: Constable Reyes's superior, Inspector Dane, whose father led the original cover-up. Dane takes Ada hostage above the sluice gates, demanding the ledger pages. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: the climax's held breath — water rising, truth demanded.

chapters.title: The Final Entry
chapters.summary: Ada stalls Dane by reading the ledger aloud — naming every payee, every sum, every year — until Reyes and the payees themselves arrive, choosing exposure over complicity. Dane slips into the weir; Reyes chooses to save him, breaking the cycle. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: catharsis; secrets spoken lose their teeth.

chapters.title: Alphabetized at Last
chapters.summary: Weeks later, testimony given and the drowned man properly buried, Ada reopens the shop with Edith beside her and Colm shelving books. She files the ledger under 'H' for Hawley — history, not leverage — and locks the door on it. POV: Ada. Emotional beat: belonging earned honestly at last.
